interactions.label: A 40-year-old man with a tibial shaft malunion has supine anteroposterior and la

params.question: A 40-year-old man with a tibial shaft malunion has supine anteroposterior and lateral radiographs showing an apparently acceptable 4° valgus angulation. His orthopaedic surgeon orders additional imaging before planning management. Which limitation of the initial radiographs justifies this decision?

answers.text: Supine radiographs cannot include the joints above and below the fracture on a single cassette

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Long-leg cassettes can include the joints above and below even when taken supine. The limitation is in how accurately they represent alignment under physiological loading, not in field coverage.

answers.text: Supine films underestimate functional angulation compared to long-leg weight-bearing radiographs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Standing (weight-bearing) films reveal the true functional alignment under physiological loading. Supine films underestimate the angulation because gravity and muscle forces are not acting on the limb.

answers.text: Anteroposterior views are unable to demonstrate valgus deformity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: AP views do demonstrate valgus and varus deformity in the coronal plane. The issue here is the patient's position — supine versus standing — not the radiographic projection.

answers.text: Plain radiography cannot measure angular deformity in more than one plane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Standard AP and lateral films measure angulation in two planes (coronal and sagittal). The difficulty with plain radiography lies in quantifying rotational malunion, which requires CT scanogram — not in measuring angular deformity.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: for lower-limb malunion, standing (weight-bearing) long-leg films are mandatory because supine radiographs underestimate the real angulation the patient experiences on walking. CT scanogram is added when rotational malunion is suspected.
Well done. Long-leg standing radiographs are mandatory for lower-limb malunion because supine films underestimate the true functional angulation the patient experiences during weight-bearing.

interactions.label: A fracture is classified as open only when bone is visibly protruding through th

params.question: A fracture is classified as open only when bone is visibly protruding through the skin.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The defining criterion is communication between the fracture haematoma and the external environment through a breach in the overlying soft tissues — not visible bone protrusion. Even a small puncture wound overlying a fracture makes it open because contamination can reach the fracture site.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. An open fracture is defined as any fracture where the overlying skin and soft tissues are breached, allowing the fracture haematoma to communicate with the external environment. Even a 1 cm puncture wound with no visible bone qualifies as an open fracture.

interactions.label: A 22-year-old man with a Grade II open tibial fracture arrives in the emergency

params.question: A 22-year-old man with a Grade II open tibial fracture arrives in the emergency department. The surgical registrar plans to defer antibiotics until the patient reaches the operating theatre for debridement within 6 hours. Based on current evidence, what is the correct approach?

answers.text: The registrar's plan is correct — surgical debridement within 6 hours is the primary determinant of infection risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 6-hour debridement rule is now considered obsolete. Current evidence identifies the timing of antibiotic administration — not debridement — as the primary modifiable determinant of infection risk in open fractures.

answers.text: Administer antibiotics immediately in the emergency department, within 1 hour of presentation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The 1-hour antibiotic window is the current evidence-based standard. Bacteria colonise devascularised tissue rapidly, and deferring antibiotics to the operating theatre multiplies infection risk in a way that no degree of later surgical debridement can fully reverse.

answers.text: Prioritise wound irrigation and debridement first; antibiotic timing is less important if thorough debridement is performed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wound care is one of the three immediate priorities, but antibiotic timing is the single most important modifiable risk factor. All three — antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, and wound care — must be initiated in the emergency department, not deferred to the theatre.

answers.text: Defer all treatment until the fracture grade is formally confirmed by the consultant on call

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, and wound care must be initiated immediately upon clinical assessment in the emergency department. Deferring any of these three priorities multiplies the subsequent infection risk.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: antibiotics must be administered within 1 hour of presentation for open fractures — this is the current evidence-based standard that has replaced the older 'debridement within 6 hours' concept. Antibiotics, tetanus, and wound care must never be deferred to the operating theatre.
Excellent. The 1-hour antibiotic window has replaced the obsolete 6-hour debridement rule as the primary evidence-based standard for reducing infection risk in open fractures.

interactions.label: A 6-year-old child with a displaced extension-type supracondylar humerus fractur

params.question: A 6-year-old child with a displaced extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture cannot perform the 'OK sign' (tip-to-tip pinch of thumb and index finger), yet hand sensation is completely intact. Which nerve is most likely injured, and what explains the preserved sensation?

answers.text: Ulnar nerve — its motor fibres to the hand intrinsics are superficial and vulnerable, while sensory fibres are protected

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ulnar nerve injury presents with weakness of finger abduction and adduction, and sensory loss over the ulnar one-and-a-half digits — not with isolated loss of the OK sign with fully intact sensation.

answers.text: Anterior interosseous nerve — a pure motor branch of the median nerve that carries no sensory fibres

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The AIN is the most commonly injured nerve in extension-type supracondylar fractures. It innervates flexor pollicis longus and the index finger flexor digitorum profundus (both needed for the OK sign) but carries only motor fibres, so sensation remains completely intact.

answers.text: Posterior interosseous nerve — a pure motor branch of the radial nerve controlling wrist and finger extension

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PIN injury causes finger drop and wrist drop (with radial deviation), not loss of the pinch mechanism. The OK sign specifically tests AIN-innervated muscles (FPL and index FDP), not radial nerve territory.

answers.text: Median nerve trunk — the motor fascicles are selectively injured while the sensory fascicles escape due to their deeper position

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Selective fascicular injury within the median nerve trunk is uncommon in paediatric blunt trauma. The clinical picture of pure motor loss with intact sensation points specifically to the AIN, which branches off as a purely motor nerve in the proximal forearm.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) is the most commonly injured nerve in extension-type supracondylar fractures. It supplies FPL and the index FDP (tested by the OK sign) but carries no sensory fibres — that is why sensation is spared despite motor loss.

Well done. The anterior interosseous nerve — a purely motor branch of the median nerve — is the most commonly injured nerve in supracondylar fractures. Always test the OK sign; preserved sensation confirms AIN rather than median nerve trunk injury.
